name: Ted Kaczynski
role: American mathematician and anti-technology writer; the 'Unabomber' (1942-2023)
summary: He argued that industrial-technological society cannot be reformed, that it destroys human autonomy, dignity and wild nature, and that it must be brought down by a revolution aimed at technology and the economy rather than at governments. He rejected the left as a movement driven by inferiority feelings and oversocialization and refused collaboration with it, and he defended revolutionary violence, which he carried out in a 1978-1995 mail-bomb campaign that killed three people. On most conventional questions (economy, immigration, social issues) he took no recorded position.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: ISAIF para. 1 holds that the Industrial Revolution and its technological development have been a disaster and that further development will worsen matters; para. 170 mocks the promise that science will fix famine and psychological suffering.

accelerate-technology.rationale: His stated aim is to halt and dismantle technological development (ISAIF paras. 4, 166, 179: 'dump the whole stinking system'), the opposite of speeding it up.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Opens ISAIF with the claim that the Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster for the human race, damaging society, human dignity and the natural world.

revolution-justified.rationale: Advocated a revolution against the industrial system (ISAIF para. 4) and in Anti-Tech Revolution says revolutionaries should aim for the system's collapse 'by any means necessary'.

political-violence-never.rationale: ISAIF para. 96 says that to get their message heard 'we've had to kill people'; in 'Morality and Revolution' he argues revolution against the technoindustrial system is justified even though it violates fairness and costs innocent lives, comparing it to World War II. His bombing campaign (1978-1995) was the practice.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: In 'Morality and Revolution' he states revolution 'will violate human decency and the principles of fairness' and that one may have to commit injustice and cruelty to prevent a greater evil; he rejected conventional morality for revolutionaries.

human-enhancement.rationale: ISAIF paras. 122-124, 154-160 oppose genetic and biological engineering of people; he argues the only ethics code that would protect freedom is one prohibiting any genetic engineering of human beings.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: ISAIF para. 50 calls conservatives fools for lamenting decayed traditional values while backing technological progress: rapid technological change inevitably breaks down traditional values, so the two cannot be combined.

algorithmic-government.rationale: ISAIF paras. 172-174 warn that if machines take over decisions, human fate is at their mercy, or control passes to a tiny elite; he does not welcome more algorithmic governance.

automate-paid-work.rationale: ISAIF paras. 172-176 argue that machines doing all work leaves people either at the machines' mercy or kept busy with make-work, and that lack of real effort-demanding goals harms people (the 'power process').

surveillance-ok.rationale: Lists surveillance devices, computers and invasion of privacy among technological threats to freedom (ISAIF paras. 95, 130, 147) and says surveillance makes physical coercion more effective.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: ISAIF paras. 63-65, 80-82, 86 describe advertising-created artificial needs and the chase for goods and status as unfulfilling surrogate activity, and say it is demeaning to meet one's need for purpose that way.

simple-living.rationale: Criticises artificial needs and dependence on the system (ISAIF paras. 63-66) and favours small-scale self-reliance (paras. 198-199); his own record was a cabin life without electricity or running water.

return-to-foraging.rationale: In a letter (Technological Slavery) he says hunting-and-gathering life was 'better beyond comparison' than modern life, and he seeks to eliminate industrial civilization; he does not lay out a plan for everyone to become foragers, and ISAIF para. 212 leaves the later course to future generations.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: ISAIF paras. 183-184 propose wild nature, independent of human management and control, as the positive ideal, and note 2 mentions the view that wild nature matters more than human economic welfare as an 'outsider' value in contrast to mainstream ones.

limit-growth.rationale: ISAIF para. 195 treats cutting back economic growth and technological progress as part of the needed worldwide revolution, and he cites environmental damage; in Anti-Tech Revolution he calls the environmental issue a 'sideshow' to eliminating the technological system, so the aim is broader than environmental protection.

limit-population.rationale: In a letter to David Skrbina he opposes a campaign for population reduction, calling it futile and counterproductive to a revolutionary movement, while allowing the movement to cite overpopulation as a consequence of technological progress.

direct-action.rationale: Says the revolution he favours 'will not be a POLITICAL revolution', focused on technology and economics, and that revolutionaries should avoid assuming political power (ISAIF paras. 4, 193-194); reform and electoral politics are judged futile (paras. 100, 111-113).

means-match-ends.rationale: Argues revolutionaries should discard conventional morality and accept violating fairness for the goal, while limiting this to what is necessary ('Morality and Revolution'); he does not hold that means must mirror the intended society.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: His campaign was a tiny group's attempt to publicise and promote an anti-technology revolution, and ISAIF paras. 181, 189 say history is made by determined minorities and call for raising social stress; but para. 167 says the system will not fall to revolutionary action alone unless its own problems lead it into crisis. Mixed, so low.

experts-over-public.rationale: Condemns control by technicians and experts: techniques 'prescribed by experts' govern lives (para. 66), and he sets the power-holding elite (politicians, scientists, executives) against the general public (para. 190).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Casts politicians as part of the power-holding elite opposed to the public (ISAIF para. 190) and lists political corruption among problems the system has failed to stop (para. 136).

decide-locally.rationale: Defines freedom as control, individually or as a member of a SMALL group, over the life-and-death issues of one's existence (para. 94) and praises small-group autonomy, while arguing it cannot survive in a technological society (paras. 117-118).

duties-before-rights.rationale: Treats emphasis on 'the duty of the individual to serve society' as a leftist trait (para. 229) and rejects the 'bourgeois' view of rights as means to collective ends (para. 97).

person-over-state.rationale: Objects that the system reduces people to 'mere cogs in the social machine' (para. 2) and rejects theories that make freedoms serve collective ends (para. 97).

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Defines freedom as being free of interference, manipulation or supervision by others, especially large organizations (para. 94), and objects that people's lives depend on remote decisions they cannot influence (paras. 67, 114).

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Treats socialization pressure as harmful (paras. 24-32, 72-73) and, in 'Morality and Revolution', criticises moralists who impose their morality on others.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: In 'Morality and Revolution' he criticises leftists who try to suppress politically incorrect speech as imposing their morality; ISAIF para. 12 is critical of political-correctness activism.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: ISAIF para. 96 says freedom of the press is of little use to the average person because mass media are controlled by large organizations and individuals' words are swamped. His emphasis is on large organizations rather than the rich as such.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Holds that the economic and technological structure of society matters more than laws or form of government for freedom (para. 95), that societies change through social evolution not rational choice (para. 106), and in letters treats technology as the independent variable.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Describes mass entertainment as an escape from stress that keeps people functioning within the system, and propaganda and media as tools of manipulation (ISAIF paras. 73, 147).

local-production.rationale: Contrasts earlier small communities that were largely self-sufficient with modern dependence on global systems (Technological Slavery letters; ISAIF paras. 117-118, 208).

shared-human-nature.rationale: Treats human nature as biological and unfit for engineering, and includes it in 'wild nature' that should be free of organized-society control (paras. 157, 183); he does not ground rights in it.

character-from-environment.rationale: Says human thought and behaviour have a largely biological basis (para. 157) and that personality traits are partly inherited (para. 204), though he also stresses socialization.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Values rationality (para. 15 lists it among things leftists hate; para. 187 wants a core opposed to the system on a rational basis) but also advises simple, emotive propaganda for the masses (para. 188).

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Criticises 'leftish philosophers' who dismiss reason, science and objective reality and insist everything is culturally relative (para. 18), while granting that questions about scientific foundations are legitimate.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Describes political-correctness activism as strongest among secure, comfortable university professors rather than the groups it claims to speak for (para. 12) and the oversocialized leftist as an intellectual or upper-middle-class type (para. 27).

traditional-family.rationale: Presents the breakdown of natural small-scale communities such as the extended family, village and tribe as an abnormal condition of industrial society (paras. 47, 51); he rejects conservative attempts to defend such values while backing technology.

taxation-theft.rationale: In a letter to Skrbina he cites compulsory taxation as a sensible collective-action arrangement that serves everyone's interest, not as theft.

property-fundamental.rationale: In 'Morality and Revolution' he says private property, as it works in modern society, lets organizations control vast resources to exert power over others and conflicts with fairness; respecting it perpetuates that system.

arms-reduction.rationale: In a text in Technological Slavery he says virtually every thinking person agrees the world would be better off without nuclear weapons and that they offer no benefits.

abortion-legal.rationale: He mentions abortion only as an example of how moral claims lend legitimacy to imposing one's will, and as an escapist cause for conservatives (Technological Slavery); he states no position on legality.

limit-guns.rationale: Lists support for gun control as a trait he attributes to leftists (ISAIF para. 229) but states no position of his own on gun ownership.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Calls gay rights a pseudo-revolutionary issue that distracts from his goal but states no view on same-sex marriage.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Says hostility to immigrants misreads migration as a consequence of technological progress, but states no preference on immigration levels (Technological Slavery).

democracy-best.rationale: Mixed: manifesto para. 117 says an individual's vote in a large electorate is negligible and para. 195 says differences between democratic and dictatorial states are small next to the industrial/non-industrial divide; Anti-Tech Revolution ch. 4 section 5 calls majority opinion irrelevant to social struggles (the 'democratic fallacy'). He never says democracy is bad.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anti-Tech Revolution ch. 2 (part IV) presents nuclear power as an environmental hazard, noting unsolved radioactive waste, and predicts the system will keep building more plants regardless; he lists it with the system's destructive energy sources.

death-penalty.rationale: Faced a federal capital charge and said he preferred risking death over life imprisonment, but states no view on the death penalty as policy (Technological Slavery).

notes:
Answers rest on his own writings; none inferred from labels. He explicitly rejected 'leftism' and said capitalism and socialism are not the cause of the technological system's constraints (ISAIF para. 119), so economic and most social statements are null. The Technological Slavery scan is OCR text; quotations were checked against the manifesto where possible.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 20 answers taken from it, 21 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Historical figure (died 10 June 2023). Anti-Tech Revolution (2016) calls for the collapse of the technological system and, for any open movement, strict legality, while the 1995 manifesto and 'Morality and Revolution' accept violence; his 2020 essay on ecofascism rejects racism as strategy. Much of his writing deliberately treats capitalism, centralisation, globalisation, big government and inequality as subordinate evils not to be fought separately (Appendix Three), so most economic and government statements are null.
